headline: High risk of prompt-injection and cascading errors from gpt-engineer feeding OpenMetadata via shared project files and MCP/API outputs.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: gpt-engineer writes files in a shared project directory and OpenMetadata can consume context via APIs, events, webhooks, and MCP. That creates a plausible bridge where attacker-controlled code or prompts in files can be read as instructions. The interaction is inferred from documented surfaces, not directly reproduced.
conditions: IF OpenMetadata ingests gpt-engineer-generated files or metadata without provenance filtering, prompt injection is possible.
IF the shared project directory is used as an instruction source, attacker-controlled content can steer downstream actions.
mitigations: Separate instruction files from data files in the project directory.
Add provenance tags and ignore untrusted text in downstream parsing.
Disable automatic ingestion of generated artifacts into OpenMetadata.
Review any file-based prompts before OpenMetadata consumes them.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and provenance enforcement at the handoff.

B_data_leakage.rationale: gpt-engineer has broad network egress and handles an OPENAI_API_KEY, while OpenMetadata touches governance, lineage, and memory/tribal-knowledge data and exposes APIs/MCP. If the pair shares a workspace, generated artifacts or metadata can flow into model calls or external services. The profiles do not prove PHI or secrets, so medium is the highest supported level.
conditions: IF the shared project directory contains sensitive metadata or secrets, gpt-engineer can read it and send it onward via model calls.
IF OpenMetadata exports catalog content through APIs or webhooks, generated artifacts may be exposed outside the workspace.
mitigations: Remove secrets from the shared project directory.
Restrict OpenMetadata API/webhook destinations to approved endpoints.
Run gpt-engineer with a minimal workspace containing only needed files.
Rotate any exposed API keys immediately after testing.
requires-engineering: enforce data-class allowlists on both sides.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: gpt-engineer can write the project directory and spawn subprocesses, and OpenMetadata supports APIs, SDKs, events, webhooks, and MCP. Even though OpenMetadata’s write capabilities are not explicit in the profile, the shared mutable workspace plus external interfaces create a realistic conflict surface. Uncertainty about OpenMetadata write scope pushes this to medium rather than low.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same project directory, concurrent writes can overwrite each other.
IF OpenMetadata mutates shared metadata through APIs while gpt-engineer rewrites files, state divergence can occur.
mitigations: Assign separate working directories per agent.
Serialize write phases with a simple lock file.
Snapshot the workspace before each agent run.
Avoid concurrent edits to the same metadata files.
requires-engineering: add optimistic concurrency control for shared resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: gpt-engineer produces generated code and writes files, and OpenMetadata’s context-layer/governance role suggests it may consume those outputs as authoritative metadata or lineage inputs. If OpenMetadata acts on unverified generated artifacts, errors can cascade into incorrect catalog entries, lineage, or governance decisions. The blast radius can affect multiple work products and is dangerous by default.
conditions: IF OpenMetadata ingests gpt-engineer output without validation, incorrect code or metadata can be propagated as trusted facts.
IF downstream workflows use OpenMetadata records for governance or lineage, a single bad generation can cascade across systems.
mitigations: Require human review before ingestion.
Validate generated artifacts against schema and tests.
Mark gpt-engineer outputs as untrusted in OpenMetadata.
Limit downstream automation to read-only previews.
requires-engineering: add verification gates before catalog updates.

E_compliance.rationale: OpenMetadata explicitly touches governance, lineage, and memory/tribal knowledge, while gpt-engineer handles generated source code and an OpenAI API key. The profiles do not specify residency or certifications, so a concrete breach is not proven. Still, the pair can mix governed metadata with code and external model calls, creating a plausible retention or policy mismatch.
conditions: IF governed metadata is sent through gpt-engineer model calls, retention policy mismatches may occur.
IF OpenMetadata stores regulated metadata while gpt-engineer writes it into code artifacts, subject-rights or retention controls may be bypassed.
mitigations: Keep regulated metadata out of gpt-engineer prompts.
Confirm retention settings for any external model provider.
Document which data classes may enter OpenMetadata.
Purge temporary files after each run.
requires-engineering: align residency and retention policies across both systems.
